title: Organ size bears no constant ratio to body size through life, especially the brain

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Organ size bears no constant ratio to body size through life, especially the brain

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: There is no simple and constant relation, holding throughout life, between the size of the whole body and that of organs such as brain, heart and liver; the brain in particular falls from about one-eighth of body weight at birth to about one-fiftieth at twenty-five.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: It is plain, then, that there is no simple and direct relation, holding good _throughout life_, between the size of the body as a whole and that of the organs we have just discussed; and the changing ratio of magnitude is especially marked in the case of the brain

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter III, “The Rate of Growth”; topic “Rate of growth of organs”. Scope: humans and other vertebrates (lion, dogfish)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch03-16: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.81

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Age, body size and organ volumes are well-defined, and public human imaging spans key developmental periods. Standard allometric models can decisively test non-constant organ ratios, even if the exact historical fractions carry measurement uncertainty.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate organ-to-body mass or volume ratios across age and test whether ratios remain constant; for brain, compare the ratio at birth and age 25 with the stated approximate fractions. Significant age-dependent allometry supports the central claim, while constant ratios refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Combining repositories introduces cohort and measurement differences.

Historical fractions may depend on mass-versus-volume conversion.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.85
operationalizability: 0.95
data existence: 0.8

analysis feasibility: 0.75

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A constant organ-to-body ratio is a sharp null, and human brain volume plus body mass by age are each publicly available, though usually not in the same file. Joining them can test the human brain fractions, which are the quantitative core of the claim. Heart, liver, and the non-human examples remain scattered, so the claim throughout life and across the vertebrates cited is only partly covered.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Plot brain, heart, and liver mass as fractions of body mass from birth to adult ages. For the human brain, the claim predicts a fall from about one-eighth of body weight at birth to about one-fiftieth at age 25. A ratio that stays constant over that span would refute the claim; the same test applied to heart, liver, lion, and dogfish needs their own series.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The lion and dogfish series are not in these human-centered archives.

MRI volume and autopsy weight are not the same quantity, and body mass is often not in the imaging file.
